# Dark mode is here

Dark mode ships today in version 3.2, on every platform we support.

We got asked for this a lot. The request usually arrived in one of two forms: someone writing at 1 a.m. who did not want a white rectangle in their face, or someone whose whole desktop was already dark and found our one bright window annoying. Both are fair. Neither took us three years to understand, which makes the wait harder to explain than the feature.

The short version of the delay: we did not want to ship an inverted color scheme and call it done. Notes are full of things that carry meaning through color, including syntax highlighting, tag chips, highlighter marks, and the diff view in version history. Flip the background and half of those become unreadable. So we rebuilt the palette from the ground rather than subtracting from the light one, then checked every combination against WCAG AA contrast. A few of our old tag colors did not survive. If your yellow tag looks slightly different now, that is why.

To turn it on, open Settings, then Appearance. You get three options: Light, Dark, and Match System. Match System follows your OS setting, so notes go dark at sunset if your machine does.

Two things worth knowing. Images and PDFs you embed are left alone, since dimming them tends to look worse than the contrast it fixes. And exported PDFs still print light, because your printer will thank you.

Tell us what looks wrong. We expect to find edges we missed.

---

# Dark mode, finally

Dark mode ships today in version 3.2. Open Settings → Appearance, or let it follow your system — it switches at sunset if macOS or Windows says so.

It took us fourteen months. That's embarrassing for what people assume is a CSS variable swap, so here's what ate the time.

Inverting a note-taking app is mostly a typography problem. White text on pure black smears at small sizes; your eye chases the halo instead of the letterform. We landed on #1A1A1E for the canvas and a warm off-white at 87% opacity for body copy, which tested at a 13:1 contrast ratio without the glare. Headings go brighter. Quiet metadata — timestamps, tag counts, word count — drops to 60% and stops competing.

Then there were the images. Paste a screenshot with a white background into a dark note and it detonates. We now dim inline images by 8% until you hover, and you can turn that off per-note if you're a designer who needs true color.

Code blocks got their own palette rather than an inverted version of the light one. Syntax highlighting that reads well on paper reads like a Christmas tree at night.

Four things we didn't do: no AMOLED pure-black variant, no per-notebook themes, no scheduled toggle beyond the system setting, no custom accent colors. All four are on the list. The pure-black one is next, because roughly a third of you asked for it by name.

Update from the App Store or run the in-app updater. Tell us what looks wrong.

rows.prompt: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

## The three-hour outage nobody could explain

Checkout was failing for about 4% of users. Not all of them. Four percent. The dashboards were green: CPU fine, memory fine, and the error rate at the API gateway had crept from 0.1% to 0.4% without tripping anything, because the alert threshold was set at 1%.

It took three engineers most of an afternoon to find it. A connection pool in the payments service, sized at 20 back in 2019 and never revisited, saturating whenever a nightly batch job overlapped with the European morning rush.

Here is the part worth sitting with. Every piece of information needed to diagnose that in ninety seconds already existed inside the running system. It simply wasn't reachable. The pool exposed a gauge; nothing scraped it. The failing requests carried a trace ID; nothing joined that ID to the payments logs. The system was talking. No one had wired up the ears.

That gap, between what your software knows about itself and what you can actually ask it, is what observability means. Monitoring answers the questions you thought of in advance. Observability is what you have left when the question is new, which during an incident it always is.

Most teams treat this as a purchase. Pick the vendor, ship the agent, tick the box. But instrumenting a system is a design activity, and it belongs next to the code, made by the people who know which failure modes are plausible and which are fantasy.

---

**Your dashboards are green. Checkout is broken.**

Every team I've worked with has monitoring. CPU, memory, request rate, a p99 latency graph that someone set up in 2021 and nobody has touched since. Then checkout starts failing for 3% of users — Android only, Brazil only, only when the coupon field isn't empty — and not one of those graphs so much as twitches. The pager stays quiet. Support finds out first, from a customer.

That gap has a name, and it isn't "we need more dashboards."

Monitoring answers the questions you thought to ask in advance. You predicted a failure, you built a chart for it, the chart tells you when it happens. Observability is whether you can answer the question you *didn't* predict — at 2 a.m., from data you already collected, without shipping a new log line and waiting forty minutes for a deploy.

Most outages live in that second category. The known failure modes get runbooks and alerts within a week of the first incident. What actually burns your on-call is the unknown one: some interaction between a retry policy, a cache eviction, and a customer who does something nobody imagined. You can't pre-build a graph for that. You can only make your system answerable.

The practical difference shows up in how long an incident takes. Teams that can slice their traffic by user, region, version, and feature flag find the coupon-field bug in ten minutes. Teams reading aggregate dashboards spend three hours guessing, then add a log line and wait.

gated.text:
## You can't debug what you can't see

At 3:14 on a Tuesday morning, checkout starts failing for about one customer in forty. Nothing pages. The error-rate dashboard stays green, because one in forty rounds to zero against a wall of healthy traffic. You find out eleven hours later, from a support ticket written by someone who tried four times and then gave up.

The distance between "the system started misbehaving" and "a human noticed" is what observability collapses. That's not the same job as monitoring. Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask ahead of time: is the disk full, is the queue backing up, did the pod restart again. Good questions. They cover roughly the first year of a system's life. After that the failures get strange, and they live in the seam between a retry policy, a connection pool, and one customer whose payload is 400 times bigger than anyone else's.

Observability is the property that lets you ask a question nobody anticipated and answer it without shipping code. Which requests were slow? Slow in which dependency? For which tenant, on which build, holding which feature flag?

A team with that property debugs an incident in a working session. A team without it debugs by guess-and-redeploy: add a log line, wait for the bug to recur, discover the log line was in the wrong branch, repeat. The second team isn't worse at engineering. They're working blind, and blindness is expensive in a way that never shows up as a line item.

---

# A year of remote work: four things we got wrong

We sent everyone home in March and called it temporary. It wasn't.

Meetings didn't shrink. They bred. By month six our engineers had 31% more calendar hours than the year before, because every hallway question turned into a scheduled call with an agenda. What fixed it was blunt: we deleted every recurring meeting on the books and made people re-create the ones they missed. A third of them never came back.

Onboarding broke first and broke loudest. New hires took a median 42 days to ship to production, against 19 the year before. Nobody was failing them on purpose. They just had no way to overhear things. We ended up assigning each new person a named buddy with two scheduled hours a week, and the number came back down to 24.

Writing turned into the actual job. The people who thrived weren't the loudest on video; they were the ones who could leave a clear paragraph behind at 4pm for someone starting their day in Berlin. We started reviewing design docs the way we review code.

And a warning, since we learned it the expensive way: async does not mean absent. Two people quit in the same month, both citing isolation, and neither had said a word about it in a standup. We now do a monthly 1:1 that has no agenda and no project talk.

Would we go back? No. But remote is a set of habits you have to build on purpose, not a place you move to.

**A year remote: the parts we got wrong**

We went remote in March and told everyone it was temporary. It wasn't.

The first thing to break wasn't productivity. Story points held steady, which we now suspect mostly proves story points measure nothing. Onboarding broke. Our four new hires took an average of eleven weeks to ship to production; before, that number was four. Nobody overheard anything anymore. The knowledge that used to leak sideways across a desk row now had to be asked for out loud, by someone who didn't yet know the right question to ask.

So we wrote it down. All of it. Forty pages nobody wanted to write, including three paragraphs on why the billing service has two queues.

Second: meetings expand to fill the calendar. We drifted from 14 hours a week to 23 before anyone said anything, because scheduling is free and walking to a room isn't. Third, and the one we underpriced: timezone spread. A four-hour gap turns a five-minute question into a next-day question, and a next-day question into a guess. Our Lisbon and Seattle engineers weren't collaborating; they were exchanging letters.

We're still remote. Two people asked to come back to an office and we rented desks for them, which felt like a defeat for about a week and then just felt like the answer.

The honest summary of year one: we saved on rent and paid for it in context.

# One year remote, and the thing we got wrong

We closed the office last March. I braced for a focus problem — people at home, the laundry, the dog. It never showed up. What broke was everything that used to happen in the four feet between two desks.

Nobody warns you that your onboarding is verbal. Ours was. The docs read fine to the eleven people who already knew the answers, and were useless to anyone else. The four engineers we hired in the fall took about nine weeks to ship something real; the last person we onboarded in the office took three. That gap was the whole year in one number. We didn't have a remote problem. We had a we-never-wrote-anything-down problem, and the office had been quietly paying the bill.

So we wrote things down. Every architectural call now lands in a dated doc with a name on it, even the ones we reverse two weeks later. Especially those.

The other change was killing the daily standup. Fifteen minutes times nine people times five days is eleven hours a week of status theater, and it existed to make managers feel oriented. We replaced it with a written thread and one long, messy, camera-on call on Thursdays where people are allowed to be stuck out loud.

Would I go back? No. But I'd stop pretending the office was a neutral baseline we were departing from. It was a crutch, and it was load-bearing, and we didn't find out until we kicked it away.

Nobody schedules technical debt. It shows up the way weeds do — a fixture copy-pasted instead of extracted, a TODO that outlives the person who wrote it, a feature flag kept "temporarily" since 2023.

We spent most of this month arguing about ours, and the argument turned out to be worth more than the conclusion. One camp wants a cleanup sprint. The other says a sprint is just a larger version of the habit that got us here: batch the mess, defer it, then take credit for the batch.

The metaphor doesn't help much either. Debt implies you borrowed on purpose and know the interest rate. Most of what slows us down was never a decision — it was a Tuesday.

So this issue skips the moralizing. Inside: a walkthrough of the migration we abandoned halfway and why the half-state was the expensive part; notes from the team that started deleting code on Fridays and what they learned about who actually owns a module; and a short piece arguing that some debt should simply be paid off never.

That's the honest version. The dishonest version is the one where we all agree the debt was a mistake, promise to pay it down next quarter, and then ship the next thing instead. We've done that. Twice, at least.

So this month isn't a cleanup sprint. It's an inventory. Three teams went back through the parts of the codebase they dread touching and wrote down why — not "it's messy," but what specifically breaks, how long a change takes, who gets paged when it doesn't work. [Name]'s piece on the auth service is the sharpest thing I've read internally this year, and the root cause turns out to be a [2019] decision nobody here can still explain.

You'll also find a short defense of leaving debt alone. Some of it is load-bearing. Some of it lives in code we're deleting in eight months anyway, and rewriting that now is just a costlier way to delete it.

Read the inventory. Argue with it. That's the point.

---

## Ostermann Fluid Systems went from eight releases a quarter to forty a week

Ostermann builds monitoring software for municipal water utilities. Forty engineers, one large Django monolith, and until last year, a release process that ran on a shared spreadsheet and a Thursday night.

"We weren't slow because anyone worked slowly," says Priya Raghunathan, who runs platform engineering. "We were slow because a release was an *event*. Nobody schedules an event twice a week."

The team started with [Platform] in March 2025 on a single service — the alerting API, picked because it was small and nobody was frightened of it. Pipelines were defined in the repo instead of clicked together in a UI, so a broken deploy could be bisected like any other bad commit. Six weeks later they moved the billing service. The monolith took until August.

The numbers as of Q1 2026:

- Deploy frequency: 8 per quarter → 40 per week
- Lead time, merge to production: 11 days → 26 minutes
- Mean rollback: 90 minutes → 4 minutes
- Change failure rate: 14% → 9%

Not everything got easier. Staging had drifted from production for years, and the pipeline surfaced that within a week — Ostermann spent most of April fixing config drift before the rollout could continue. The integration suite, written when it ran twice a month, had to be cut from 51 minutes to 6.

"Deploying often didn't make us careful," Raghunathan says. "Doing it while it was still boring did."

# Kestrel Freight cut its release cycle from six weeks to twice a day

Kestrel Freight moves refrigerated cargo across the Midwest, and for eleven years its dispatch software shipped on a six-week train. Everything went out together. A one-line fix to a timezone bug waited behind a half-finished billing rewrite, which is how a two-hour patch turned into a two-month one.

"We weren't slow because our engineers were slow," says Dana Whitlock, who runs platform engineering there. "We were slow because we'd bundled forty changes into one bet, and nobody wanted to be the person who pushed the button."

They moved to [Platform] in March. The first month was unglamorous: splitting the pipeline per service, writing the smoke tests that had never existed, arguing about who owned the rollback. By June, dispatch was deploying on merge.

The numbers, twelve months on: 9 releases a year to roughly 450. Median lead time from commit to production went from 41 days to 26 minutes. Change failure rate crept up, 4% to 6%. But mean time to restore fell from five hours to twelve minutes, because a bad deploy is now one commit wide.

What Whitlock didn't expect was the effect on the roadmap. Small changes stopped needing a business case. A support engineer can fix a mislabeled error message on a Tuesday afternoon, and nobody schedules a meeting about it.

"Release night used to be a thing we ordered pizza for," they say. "Now it's just Thursday."

# From three weeks to twelve times a day: Kestrel Freight

Kestrel Freight builds routing software for European trucking fleets. Until last spring, it released once every three weeks, on a Thursday evening, with four engineers sitting on a rollback call.

The delay was not caution. Their test suite ran 90 minutes on a single shared machine, and failed often enough that a red build told nobody anything. Feature branches lived for weeks, and merging them was its own project. Two of the last four releases had to be backed out.

Kestrel moved to Northbound CD in March. The first month was mostly deletion. They cut 300 tests that asserted on implementation details, split the rest across parallel runners, and got the suite down to nine minutes. Per-branch preview environments meant product managers stopped queueing for staging.

"The part I did not expect was the arguments ending," says Petra Vos, their platform lead. "When a deploy costs ten minutes instead of an evening, nobody negotiates about whether a change is worth shipping."

Ten months in, they deploy 12 times a day, up from roughly one every 15 working days. Lead time from merge to production fell from 6 days to 40 minutes. Change failure rate went from 14% to 3%, mostly because a deploy now carries one change instead of three weeks of them.

Kestrel has not grown its platform team. The two engineers who used to maintain release scripts moved to the observability stack, and the Thursday call no longer exists.

**Three weeks to one day: how Meridian Freight changed its release cadence**

Meridian Freight books roughly 4,000 truckloads a week, and almost all of that runs on software its own engineers write. Until early last year, that software shipped every three weeks, on a Thursday night, with four engineers on a bridge call and a rollback plan nobody had practiced. Quarter-close weeks were off limits by rule.

"People assume we were slow because we were careful," says Dana Okonkwo, who heads platform engineering. "It was the other way round. Three weeks of changes went out at once, so of course every release was frightening."

Conveyor went in during March 2024. The first six weeks were tedious: two Rails services containerized, 140 database migrations moved behind feature flags, the test suite cut from 41 minutes to nine so a pipeline could gate a merge without anyone waiting around. Customers noticed nothing.

What came after is the story. Meridian averages 19 deploys a week now, usually mid-morning, usually pushed by whoever wrote the change. Merge to production takes 22 minutes at the median. A rollback is one click and about 90 seconds, and that, Okonkwo says, is the number that mattered. Once reverting got cheap, arguing about whether to ship got expensive.

Over the following two quarters, change failure rate went from 14% to 4%. The Thursday bridge call is gone. So is the quarter-close freeze: Meridian shipped a rate-quoting fix on the last day of Q4, at 3 p.m., with two people watching.

## Vision

In two years, shipping a service should be boring.

Right now it isn't. Standing up something new takes about six weeks from first commit to real traffic, and four of those weeks go to work nobody chose to do: wiring auth, guessing at deploy config, waiting on a staging environment that half-works, rewriting retry logic that already exists in three other repos. That's a tax. We pay it on every project and it scales with headcount, which means it gets worse exactly as we grow.

We want the paved road to be the fastest road — not the mandated one. A team that stays on it gets a service skeleton, CI, observability, on-call routing, and a tested rollback path on day one. A team that needs something else can leave the road, and owns what it picks up when it does.

The bet is simple. Work that every product team currently redoes gets pulled out of their backlogs and staffed once, properly, by people who treat it as a product with users rather than as a chore between features.

Where we want to land: median time-to-production under a week, most services on one supported runtime, and a platform team whose answers live in docs instead of DMs.

Two years, not one, because the first year is mostly subtraction. We consolidate what already exists, kill the variants nobody defends, and pay down the migration debt before we build anything new. The compounding starts in year two, and it only starts if we're honest about year one.

---

## Vision

Two years from now, a team that wants to ship a new service shouldn't have to relearn how we do deploys, secrets, tracing, and on-call. Those should arrive by default, and the team should spend its attention on the part of the problem nobody outside it can solve.

We're a long way from that. Today each team keeps a private copy of the same infrastructure decisions, drifting apart at its own rate. When a CVE lands we don't have one thing to patch; we have nineteen. When someone new joins, their first month goes to learning which of the nineteen they inherited. The cost isn't visible in any single quarter, which is exactly why it keeps growing.

So the goal for the next two years is boring on purpose: one paved road, good enough that leaving it feels like a real choice rather than the path of least resistance. A new service reaches production in a day. A dependency upgrade rolls out from one place. An engineer moving between teams recognizes the tooling on day one.

We're not aiming for a platform that handles every case. Teams with genuine reasons to go their own way should still be able to, and we'd rather earn adoption than mandate it. If the paved road only wins because we blocked the alternatives, we built the wrong road.

The measure of success isn't how much platform we've built. It's how much infrastructure work has quietly disappeared from product teams' sprints, and whether they'd notice if we took the platform away.

## Vision

Two years from now, a new service should reach production in a day, and the engineer who ships it should never have opened a Terraform file.

That is the whole bet. Right now the median new service takes eleven days from first commit to serving traffic, and roughly eight of those days are spent on work nobody wants credit for: copying a CI config from whichever neighboring repo looked healthiest, chasing IAM permissions through Slack, discovering that the metrics dashboard everyone assumed was standard was hand-built by someone who left in March. Every team pays this tax separately. We pay it about forty times a year.

We want to stop paying it forty times. The platform team's job over the next eight quarters is to make the correct path the easy one — a paved default for deploys, observability, secrets, and data access that a team adopts by doing less work, not more. Adoption is the test. If a team has to be told to use the platform, we built the wrong thing.

Concretely, by the end of the period: a service template that carries its own pipeline, alerts, and on-call routing; one deploy mechanism instead of the current four; and enough of the fleet migrated that we can retire the 2019 Jenkins cluster and the people who quietly keep it alive can go do something else.

None of this ships a feature. It buys back engineer-days at a rate we think is somewhere near 3:1, and it makes the next reorg survivable.
